categories.title: Am I allowed to?
categories.description: Written permission: a policy, consent where your rules expect it, training, vendor terms, and an approved-tool list.

categories.title: Will staff use it?
categories.description: Whether the approved tool is real, easy, and good enough, or staff still leave through a personal account.

categories.title: Is the output checked?
categories.description: Whether a person checks AI output, especially citations, before it is filed or sent.

categories.title: What goes into the tool
categories.description: What kinds of information reach an AI tool, and whether there is a written limit.

questions.prompt: Which description is closest to the business?
questions.hint: The questions, the score weights, and the rules section follow this choice. It is not sent anywhere.

choices.label: Law firm
Accounting / CPA
Healthcare practice
Bank or credit union
Other

questions.prompt: Which state's professional rules should this check use?
questions.hint: Pick the state that governs the practice, or Other if it is somewhere else. This check encodes Ohio, Kentucky, and West Virginia to start.

choices.label: Ohio
Kentucky
West Virginia
Other

questions.prompt: About how many people work in the business, including owners?

choices.label: 1 to 5
6 to 20
More than 200

questions.prompt: Which AI tools do people use for work, as far as you know?
questions.hint: Include free websites and personal accounts. This list is context for the report. The browser extension and the DNS check can look at a longer catalog on managed devices.

choices.label: ChatGPT
Claude
Gemini
Microsoft Copilot or GitHub Copilot
Perplexity
Grammarly, QuillBot, or a similar writing tool
Otter, Fireflies, Fathom, or another meeting bot
Other AI tools
None that we know of
We do not know

questions.prompt: Do you have a written policy on how staff may use AI for work?
questions.hint: A written policy is one of the things Kentucky's ethics opinion expects supervisory lawyers to have. Other states in this check do not all say the same thing. The report cites the source for the state you picked.

choices.label: Yes. It is written, and staff can find it.
We have notes or an email, not a policy people can find.

fix.title: Turn the AI notes into a written policy
fix.detail: Write who may use AI, which tools are approved, what information stays out, and who reviews output. Give every person the current copy.

choices.label: No. There is no written AI policy.

fix.title: Write an AI policy staff can find
fix.detail: Write who may use AI, which tools are approved, what information stays out, and who reviews output. Give every person the current copy.

questions.prompt: When staff put client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information into a generative AI tool, do you have a consent or approval process for the cases where your rules expect one?
questions.hint: Not every state requires consent for every use. West Virginia's advisory ethics materials say a lawyer should get informed client approval, confirmed in writing, before using generative AI. Kentucky's ethics opinion does not state a general duty to disclose ordinary AI research. Tax-return information is a separate federal rule.

choices.label: Yes. Informed consent or approval is confirmed in writing when the rules that apply to us call for it.
We do not put client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information into AI tools.
We mention AI sometimes, but consent is not informed and not confirmed in writing.

fix.title: Write the consent path your rules actually expect
fix.detail: Read the rules section of this report before you draft a form. Where consent is expected, say what the tool is, what information goes in, and what the limits are, and keep the written approval.

choices.label: No. We have no consent or approval process.

fix.title: Decide when consent is required and write it down
fix.detail: Read the rules section of this report before you draft a form. Where consent is expected, say what the tool is, what information goes in, and what the limits are, and keep the written approval.

questions.prompt: Have staff been trained on the AI policy, including what they may not put into a tool?

choices.label: Yes. Training happened in the last year, including new hires.
Some people were told once. It is not repeated for new hires.

fix.title: Train staff on the AI policy
fix.detail: Walk through the approved tools, the information that stays out, and how to check output. Repeat it for new hires. Some ethics opinions, including Kentucky's KBA E-457, treat training as part of supervising AI use.

choices.label: No. Staff have not been trained.

fix.title: Train staff on the AI policy
fix.detail: Walk through the approved tools, the information that stays out, and how to check output. Repeat it for new hires. Some ethics opinions, including Kentucky's KBA E-457, treat training as part of supervising AI use.

questions.prompt: Have you read the vendor's terms or data-processing agreement for whether it trains on client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information?
questions.hint: A SOC 2 report or a security webpage answers a different question. This one is about training and the contract, not the audit logo.

choices.label: Yes. We have terms or a data-processing agreement that say this information is not used to train their models.
We do not put that information into any AI tool, so there is nothing for a vendor to train on.
We have a SOC 2 report or a security page, and we have not checked the training terms.

fix.title: Read whether the vendor trains on client data
fix.detail: A security report does not answer this. Read the data-processing agreement or the product terms and write down whether client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information is used to train a model.

choices.label: We have not reviewed terms or a data-processing agreement.

fix.title: Read whether the vendor trains on client data
fix.detail: A security report does not answer this. Read the data-processing agreement or the product terms and write down whether client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information is used to train a model.

questions.prompt: Is there a written list of AI tools that are approved for work?

choices.label: Yes. The list is written and was looked at in the last six months.
There is a list, but it is incomplete or older than six months.

fix.title: Refresh the approved-tool list
fix.detail: Name each tool staff may use, who owns the account, and what information is off limits. Date the list and read it twice a year. The DNS check can show what the office resolver already sees.

choices.label: No. There is no approved-tool list.

fix.title: Write the approved-tool list
fix.detail: Name each tool staff may use, who owns the account, and what information is off limits. Date the list and read it twice a year. The DNS check can show what the office resolver already sees.

questions.section: Will staff use the approved tool?
questions.prompt: Is there an approved AI tool staff are supposed to use for work?
questions.hint: An approved tool on the books is not the same as a tool people actually open. The next questions are about that gap.

choices.label: Yes. There is a named tool on an account the firm controls.
People were told a tool is fine, but the firm does not own the account.

fix.title: Put the approved tool on an account you control
fix.detail: Name one tool for ordinary work and issue the accounts yourself. If you cannot close the login when someone leaves, it is not yet an approved tool.

choices.label: No. There is no approved tool.

fix.title: Name an approved AI tool
fix.detail: Pick one tool for ordinary work, issue the accounts yourself, and tell staff that other tools are not for client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information.

questions.section: Will staff use the approved tool?
questions.prompt: Is that approved tool easy enough, and good enough, that staff can finish ordinary work in it?

choices.label: Yes. Staff can do ordinary tasks in it without a workaround.
It works for some tasks. For others, people say it is too slow, blocked, or weak.

fix.title: Make the approved tool good enough for ordinary work
fix.detail: Ask which tasks send people to a personal account. If the approved tool is blocked, slow, or missing a feature they use every day, fix that before you add another rule.

choices.label: No. People work around it because it is hard to use or not good enough.

fix.title: Make the approved tool good enough for ordinary work
fix.detail: Ask which tasks send people to a personal account. If the approved tool is blocked, slow, or missing a feature they use every day, fix that before you add another rule.

choices.label: There is no approved tool to judge.

fix.title: Name an approved AI tool
fix.detail: Pick one tool for ordinary work, issue the accounts yourself, and tell staff that other tools are not for client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information.

questions.section: Will staff use the approved tool?
questions.prompt: Do staff still use personal AI accounts for work?
questions.hint: Personal accounts include a free login someone opened themselves, even if an approved tool already exists.

choices.label: No. Work stays on accounts the firm issued.
Rarely. We have seen it and we dealt with the person.
Some people still use a personal account for work.

fix.title: Close the personal-account path
fix.detail: If an approved tool exists, ask why staff still open a personal account. Fix the approved tool if it is slow or blocked, and say what happens when work goes through a personal login.

choices.label: This is normal. Personal accounts are how a lot of work gets done.

fix.title: Close the personal-account path
fix.detail: If an approved tool exists, ask why staff still open a personal account. Fix the approved tool if it is slow or blocked, and say what happens when work goes through a personal login.

choices.label: We do not know.

fix.title: Find out who still uses a personal AI account
fix.detail: Ask each person, including owners, whether work goes through a login the firm did not issue. Write down the answer and decide what happens next time.

questions.section: Will staff use the approved tool?
questions.prompt: If someone uses an unapproved tool or a personal account for work, is there a known norm or consequence?

choices.label: Yes. Staff know it is outside the policy, and a named person follows up.
People know it is frowned on. Nothing specific happens.

fix.title: Say what happens when work leaves the approved tool
fix.detail: Write the follow-up in the policy: who is told, what the person is asked to stop, and when a client or customer must be told. A rule with no follow-up is easy to ignore.

choices.label: No. There is no norm and no consequence.

fix.title: Say what happens when work leaves the approved tool
fix.detail: Write the follow-up in the policy: who is told, what the person is asked to stop, and when a client or customer must be told. A rule with no follow-up is easy to ignore.

questions.prompt: What kinds of information have gone into an AI tool for work?
questions.hint: Count personal accounts and free websites. Select every kind that applies.

choices.label: Public information or our own marketing text
Internal notes that are not client, patient, or customer records
Client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information

fix.title: Stop pasting client information into unapproved tools
fix.detail: Until the approved tool's terms say what happens to that information, keep client, patient, customer, and taxpayer records out of personal accounts and consumer chat sites.

choices.label: Social Security numbers, account numbers, card numbers, or treatment details

fix.title: Keep regulated identifiers out of AI prompts
fix.detail: Tell staff that Social Security numbers, account and card numbers, and treatment details do not go into an AI tool. This helps reduce risk. It does not settle HIPAA or any other duty.

choices.label: We do not know what people paste

fix.title: Find out what information reaches AI tools
fix.detail: Ask each person what they paste, including into personal accounts. Write the answer down and decide what stays out before the next matter or filing.

choices.label: Nothing. We do not put work information into AI tools.

questions.prompt: Is there a written rule that client, patient, customer, or taxpayer information stays out of unapproved AI tools?

choices.label: Yes. It is written in the policy staff can find.
People have been told. It is not written.

fix.title: Write the rule for client information
fix.detail: Add one paragraph to the AI policy: which information never goes into an unapproved tool, and which approved tool, if any, may receive it.

choices.label: No. There is no rule.

fix.title: Write the rule for client information
fix.detail: Add one paragraph to the AI policy: which information never goes into an unapproved tool, and which approved tool, if any, may receive it.

questions.prompt: Before a filing or a client communication that used generative AI goes out, does a lawyer review the draft?
questions.hint: This section is for law firms. A person, not the tool, is responsible for what is filed or sent.

choices.label: Yes. A lawyer reviews every such draft before it goes out.
Sometimes. It depends on who is busy.

fix.title: Review AI drafts before they are filed or sent
fix.detail: Assign a lawyer to read the draft, the facts, and the citations before a filing or client communication goes out. Kentucky, West Virginia, and Ohio materials in this check all treat a human review as part of competent use.

choices.label: No. Drafts go out without that review.

fix.title: Review AI drafts before they are filed or sent
fix.detail: Assign a lawyer to read the draft, the facts, and the citations before a filing or client communication goes out. Kentucky, West Virginia, and Ohio materials in this check all treat a human review as part of competent use.

questions.prompt: Are citations, quotations, and legal propositions from an AI tool checked against the source by a person before they are filed or sent?
questions.hint: Courts have sanctioned filings that relied on citations a generative tool invented. KBA E-457 cites Mata v. Avianca as one example from another jurisdiction. This question does not predict a sanction in your court.

choices.label: Yes. A person opens the source and checks it every time.
Sometimes, if the citation looks important.

fix.title: Check citations before anything is filed or sent
fix.detail: Have a person open the cited source and confirm the quotation and the proposition. Courts have sanctioned filings that relied on citations a generative tool invented. This step helps reduce that risk. It does not predict what a court will do.

choices.label: No. Citations are not checked against the source.

fix.title: Check citations before anything is filed or sent
fix.detail: Have a person open the cited source and confirm the quotation and the proposition. Courts have sanctioned filings that relied on citations a generative tool invented. This step helps reduce that risk. It does not predict what a court will do.

questions.prompt: Before an AI-assisted return, schedule, or client memo is filed or delivered, does a person check the facts, figures, and any citations?
questions.hint: IRS Office of Professional Responsibility guidance applies existing Circular 230 diligence and competence duties to generative AI in this way. Circular 230 has no separate AI section.

choices.label: Yes. A person checks facts, figures, and citations every time.
Sometimes. It depends on the return.

fix.title: Review AI-assisted tax work before it goes out
fix.detail: Have a person check the facts, the figures, and any citations before a return or memo is filed or delivered. IRS guidance applies Circular 230 diligence and competence duties to generative AI. This check does not decide that a duty was met.

choices.label: No. That review is not part of the process.

fix.title: Review AI-assisted tax work before it goes out
fix.detail: Have a person check the facts, the figures, and any citations before a return or memo is filed or delivered. IRS guidance applies Circular 230 diligence and competence duties to generative AI. This check does not decide that a duty was met.
